paragraphs:
Childe Rowland and his two brothers
Were playing with a ball,
And there was their sister Burd Ellen
In the middle of them all.

Childe Rowland kicked it with his foot
And caught it with his knee;
At last, as he rushed among them all,
He sent it flying over the church.

Burd Ellen went around the aisle
To search for the ball,
But long they waited, and longer still,
And she did not come back again.

They searched for her east, they searched for her west,
They searched both up and down,
And sorrow filled the hearts of those brothers,
For she could not be found.

At last her eldest brother went to the Warlock Merlin, told him the whole story, and asked whether he knew where Burd Ellen was. “The beautiful Burd Ellen,” said the Warlock Merlin, “must have been carried off by the fairies because she went around the church anticlockwise—the opposite direction to the sun. She is now in the Dark Tower of the King of Elfland. It would take the boldest knight in Christendom to bring her back.”
“If it is possible to bring her back,” her brother said, “I will do it, or die in the attempt.”
“It is possible,” said the Warlock Merlin, “but disaster awaits any man or mother’s son who attempts it without first being properly taught what to do.”

No fear of danger could put Burd Ellen’s eldest brother off trying to bring her back. He begged the Warlock Merlin to tell him what he should do, and what he should not do, when he went to seek his sister. After he had been taught and had repeated his lesson, he set out for Elfland.

But long they waited, and longer still,
With doubt and great pain,
And sorrow filled his brothers’ hearts,
For he did not come back again.
Then the second brother grew sick and tired of waiting. He went to the Warlock Merlin and asked him the same questions as his brother. Then he set out to find Burd Ellen.

But long they waited, and longer still,
With great doubt and pain,
And grief filled his mother’s and brother’s hearts,
For he did not come back again.

After they had waited and waited a good long time, Childe Rowland, the youngest of Burd Ellen’s brothers, wanted to go. He went to his mother, the good queen, and asked her to let him. At first she refused, for he was the last of her children she still had, and if he were lost, all would be lost. But he begged and begged, until at last the good queen let him go. She gave him his father’s good sword, which never struck in vain. As she fastened it around his waist, she spoke the spell that would give it victory.

Childe Rowland said goodbye to the good queen, his mother, and went to the Warlock Merlin’s cave. “Once more, and only once more,” he said to the Warlock, “tell me how any man or mother’s son can rescue Burd Ellen and her two brothers.”

“Well, my son,” said the Warlock Merlin, “there are only two things. They may seem simple, but they are hard to do. One thing to do, and one thing not to do. Here is what you must do: once you have entered the land of Fairy, until you meet Burd Ellen, you must draw your father’s sword and cut off the head of anyone who speaks to you. And here is what you must not do: eat not a bite and drink not a drop, however hungry or thirsty you are. If you drink a drop or eat a bite while you are in Elfland, you will never see Middle Earth again.”

Childe Rowland repeated the two things over and over until he knew them by heart. He thanked the Warlock Merlin and went on his way. And he went along, and along, and along, and still further along, until he came to the King of Elfland’s horse-keeper, feeding his horses. He recognised the horses by their fiery eyes and knew that he was at last in the land of Fairy. “Can you tell me,” Childe Rowland asked the horse-keeper, “where the King of Elfland’s Dark Tower is?” “I cannot tell you,” said the horse-keeper, “but go a little further, and you will come to the cowherd. Perhaps he can tell you.”

Without another word, Childe Rowland drew the good sword that never struck in vain, and off went the horse-keeper’s head. Childe Rowland went further until he came to the cowherd, and asked him the same question. “I cannot tell you,” he said, “but go a little further, and you will come to the woman who tends the hens. She is sure to know.” Then Childe Rowland drew his good sword that never struck in vain, and off went the cowherd’s head. He went a little further until he came to an old woman in a grey cloak, and asked whether she knew where the King of Elfland’s Dark Tower was. “Go a little further,” said the woman who tended the hens, “until you reach a round green hill, surrounded by rings of terraces from bottom to top. Walk around it three times, anticlockwise, and each time say:

Open, door! Open, door!
And let me come in.

and the third time, the door will open, and you may go in.” Childe Rowland was just about to go when he remembered what he had to do. So he drew the good sword that never struck in vain, and off went the woman’s head.
Then he went on, and on, and on, until he came to the round green hill with the rings of terraces from top to bottom. He walked around it three times, anticlockwise, saying each time:

Open, door! Open, door!
And let me come in.
The third time, the door did open. He went in, and it closed with a click, leaving Childe Rowland in the dark.

It was not exactly dark, but a kind of twilight or dusk. There were no windows or candles, and he could not work out where the twilight came from, unless it shone through the walls and roof. These were rough arches made of transparent rock, encrusted with mica, crystalline spar and other bright stones. But although it was rock, the air was quite warm, as it always is in Elfland. He walked along the passage until at last he came to a pair of wide, high folding doors standing partly open. When he opened them, he saw a most wonderful and glorious sight. There was a large, spacious hall, so large that it seemed as long and as broad as the green hill itself. The roof rested on fine pillars, so enormous and lofty that a cathedral’s pillars were nothing beside them. They were entirely of gold and silver, with delicate carved work. Between and around them hung wreaths of flowers made of—what do you think? Why, diamonds and emeralds and all kinds of precious stones. Even the keystones of the arches were decorated with clusters of diamonds, rubies, pearls and other precious stones. All the arches met in the middle of the roof. Just there, hanging from a gold chain, was an immense lamp made from one great pearl, hollowed out and completely transparent. In its centre was a great, huge red gemstone, spinning round and round. Its rays lit the entire hall, which looked as though the setting sun were shining upon it.

The hall’s furnishings were equally grand. At one end stood a glorious couch of velvet, silk and gold, and there sat Burd Ellen, combing her golden hair with a silver comb. When she saw Childe Rowland, she stood and said:

“God pity you, poor unlucky fool,
What have you come here to do?

“Hear this, my youngest brother,
Why didn’t you stay at home?
Even if you had a hundred thousand lives,
You couldn’t spare a single one.

“But sit down; yet grief, oh, grief,
That you were ever born,
For when the King of Elfland comes,
Your fate will be hopeless.”

They sat down together. Childe Rowland told her everything he had done, and she told him how their two brothers had reached the Dark Tower, but had been enchanted by the King of Elfland and lay there entombed as though dead. After they had talked a little longer, Childe Rowland began to feel hungry from his long travels. He told his sister Burd Ellen how hungry he was and asked for food, forgetting all about the Warlock Merlin’s warning.

Burd Ellen looked sadly at Childe Rowland and shook her head, but she was under a spell and could not warn him. She got up and went out, and soon returned with a golden basin full of bread and milk. Childe Rowland was just about to lift it to his lips when he looked at his sister and remembered why he had come all that way. He dashed the bowl to the ground and said, “I will not swallow a sip or take a bite until Burd Ellen is set free.”
Just then they heard someone approaching, and a loud voice said:

“Fee, fi, fo, fum,
I smell the blood of a Christian man,
Dead or alive, with my sword,
I’ll smash his brains out of his skull.”
Then the hall’s folding doors burst open, and the King of Elfland rushed in.

“Strike, then, goblin, if you dare!” Childe Rowland shouted, rushing to meet him with his good sword that had never yet failed. They fought, and they fought, and they fought, until Childe Rowland beat the King of Elfland down onto his knees and forced him to surrender and beg for mercy. “I grant you mercy,” Childe Rowland said. “Release my sister from your spells, bring my brothers back to life, and let us all go free, and you will be spared.” “I agree,” said the Elfin King. He rose and went to a chest, from which he took a small bottle filled with a blood-red liquid. He rubbed it on the ears, eyelids, nostrils, lips and fingertips of the two brothers. They sprang to life at once and declared that their souls had been away but had now returned. The Elfin King then spoke some words to Burd Ellen, and her enchantment was broken. All four of them left the hall, went through the long passage, and turned their backs on the Dark Tower, never to return. They reached home and the good queen, their mother, and Burd Ellen never walked around a church anticlockwise again.
